courses.title: Basic Electronics
courses.subject: Electronics
courses.description: Ohm's law, resistor networks, diodes and rectifiers for first-year B.Tech and diploma students.

lessons.title: Ohm's Law and Power
lessons.notes:
# Ohm's Law and Power
Ohm's law states that the current through a conductor is directly proportional to the voltage across it, at constant temperature.
Ohm's law: V = IR
- V is the voltage in volts (V), I is the current in amperes (A) and R is the resistance in ohms (Ω).
Electrical power is the rate at which electrical energy is used or converted.
Power: P = VI
Using Ohm's law, power can also be written in two more forms.
P = I^2 R
P = V^2 / R
Electrical energy is power multiplied by time.
Energy: E = P × t
Example: a 12 V battery drives 2 A through a lamp. The power is P = 12 × 2 = 24 W.

lessons.title: Series and Parallel Resistors
lessons.notes:
# Series and Parallel Resistors
Resistors in series carry the same current, and the total resistance is the sum of all resistances.
Series: R = R1 + R2 + R3
Resistors in parallel have the same voltage across them.
Parallel: 1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3
For only two resistors in parallel the product-over-sum rule is used.
Two in parallel: R = (R1 × R2) / (R1 + R2)
The resistance of a wire depends on its length, area and material.
Resistance of a wire: R = ρL/A
- ρ is the resistivity in Ω·m, L is the length in metres and A is the cross-sectional area in m².
Example: two 6 Ω resistors in parallel give R = (6 × 6) / (6 + 6) = 3 Ω.

lessons.title: Kirchhoff's Laws
lessons.notes:
# Kirchhoff's Laws
Kirchhoff's Current Law (KCL) states that the total current entering a node equals the total current leaving it.
KCL: ΣI_in = ΣI_out
Kirchhoff's Voltage Law (KVL) states that the algebraic sum of all voltages around a closed loop is zero.
KVL: ΣV = 0
KCL is based on conservation of charge, and KVL is based on conservation of energy.
Example: a 12 V source with 2 Ω and 4 Ω in series gives I = 12 / 6 = 2 A, so 12 − 4 − 8 = 0.

lessons.title: PN Junction Diode
lessons.notes:
# PN Junction Diode
A PN junction diode is a two-terminal device that allows current mainly in one direction.
- Forward bias: P side to positive, N side to negative. The depletion region narrows and current flows.
- Reverse bias: P side to negative, N side to positive. The depletion region widens and only a tiny leakage current flows.
The knee voltage is about 0.7 V for silicon and 0.3 V for germanium.
Diode current equation: I = I_0 (e^{V/ηV_T} − 1)
Thermal voltage: V_T = kT/q
At room temperature V_T is about 26 mV.

lessons.title: Rectifiers
lessons.notes:
# Rectifiers
A rectifier converts AC into pulsating DC.
## Half-wave rectifier
A half-wave rectifier uses one diode and passes only one half cycle.
Half-wave DC voltage: V_dc = V_m / π
Half-wave ripple factor: γ = 1.21
## Full-wave rectifier
A full-wave rectifier passes both half cycles in the same direction through the load.
Full-wave DC voltage: V_dc = 2V_m / π
Full-wave ripple factor: γ = 0.482
Full-wave efficiency: η = 81.2 %
The bridge rectifier uses four diodes and does not need a centre-tapped transformer.

courses.title: Physics: Motion and Energy
courses.subject: Physics
courses.description: Equations of motion, Newton's laws, work, energy and power.

lessons.title: Equations of Motion
lessons.notes:
# Equations of Motion
These equations apply when the acceleration is uniform.
- u is the initial velocity, v is the final velocity, a is the acceleration, t is the time and s is the displacement.
The first equation of motion relates velocity and time.
v = u + at
The second equation of motion gives displacement in time t.
s = ut + ½at²
The third equation of motion relates velocity and displacement.
v² = u² + 2as
Example: a car starts from rest and accelerates at 2 m/s² for 5 s. Its final velocity is v = 0 + 2 × 5 = 10 m/s.

lessons.title: Newton's Laws, Work and Energy
lessons.notes:
# Newton's Laws, Work and Energy
Newton's second law states that force equals mass times acceleration.
Newton's second law: F = ma
Momentum is the product of mass and velocity.
Momentum: p = mv
Work is done when a force moves an object in the direction of the force.
Work: W = F × s
Kinetic energy is the energy of a moving body.
Kinetic energy: KE = ½mv²
Potential energy is the energy due to height.
Potential energy: PE = mgh
Power is the rate of doing work.
Power: P = W / t

courses.title: Chemistry: Reactions and Gases
courses.subject: Chemistry
courses.description: Balanced chemical equations, the gas laws and solution concentration.

lessons.title: Balanced Chemical Equations
lessons.notes:
# Balanced Chemical Equations
A balanced chemical equation has the same number of atoms of each element on both sides.
Hydrogen burns in oxygen to form water.
2H2 + O2 → 2H2O
Calcium carbonate decomposes on heating to give calcium oxide and carbon dioxide.
CaCO3 → CaO + CO2
Methane burns in oxygen to give carbon dioxide and water.
CH4 + 2O2 → CO2 + 2H2O
Iron reacts with copper sulphate solution in a displacement reaction.
Fe + CuSO4 → FeSO4 + Cu

lessons.title: Gas Laws and Molarity
lessons.notes:
# Gas Laws and Molarity
Boyle's law states that at constant temperature, pressure is inversely proportional to volume.
Boyle's law: P1V1 = P2V2
Charles's law states that at constant pressure, volume is directly proportional to absolute temperature.
Charles's law: V1/T1 = V2/T2
The ideal gas equation combines the gas laws.
Ideal gas equation: PV = nRT
- R is the gas constant, 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.
Molarity is the number of moles of solute per litre of solution.
Molarity: M = n / V
pH measures how acidic a solution is.
pH = −log[H+]
